title: How Much of a Harness Does a Strong Agent Need for Autonomous ML Engineering
content:
How Much of a Harness Does a Strong Agent Need for Autonomous ML Engineering?
AuthorsKirill Brilliantov†‡, Alejandro Hernández-Cano†‡**, Emmanuel Abbé†
Recent autonomous machine learning engineering (MLE) agents have made significant progress on public leaderboards. Often motivated by progress stagnation over long-horizon cycles and limited Large Language Model (LLM) primitives, modern MLE agents are deployed on top of increasingly elaborate machinery: multi-agent orchestrators, dedicated retrieval subagents, and more. While such harnesses expand, the use of more primitive but improved coding agents—where LLMs have direct access to the execution environment through read, write, and bash primitives—has received little attention in the field. In this paper we find that, under an equal time budget and the same frontier LLM backbone, open-source state-of-the-art harnesses provide no advantages over a single session of a minimal-harness coding agent baseline, pointing to the backbone as the primary driver for performance. Via a series of large-scale systematic ablation studies, we argue that the machinery layers become redundant in the coding agent setting. We conclude that the effort spent elaborating hand-crafted harnesses around strong models yields poor returns for current MLE benchmarks.

report.summary: Apple researchers find that, given the same strong LLM and equal time, elaborate agent harnesses offer no advantage over a minimal coding-agent setup for autonomous ML engineering.
report.background: Autonomous machine learning engineering (MLE) agents have improved rapidly on public leaderboards. Because long-horizon tasks can stagnate and LLM primitives are limited, many builders add elaborate machinery: multi-agent orchestrators, retrieval subagents, memory systems, and custom prompting layers. Meanwhile, simpler coding agents that give LLMs direct read, write, and bash access to an execution environment have become stronger. This paper tests whether the elaborate harness actually matters when the underlying model and time budget are held constant. The question is important because harness engineering is expensive and can distract teams from model capability, evaluation design, and reliable tool interfaces. If a minimal coding-agent baseline matches state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, then much of the current scaffolding work may be poor return on effort for today's MLE benchmarks.
key_points: Under an equal time budget and the same frontier LLM backbone, open-source state-of-the-art harnesses showed no advantage over a single-session minimal-harness coding agent. The minimal baseline, which relies on read, write, and bash primitives, was enough to match more elaborate systems.

The paper points to the LLM backbone as the primary driver of performance. Large-scale systematic ablation studies suggest that orchestration, retrieval, and other machinery layers become largely redundant when a strong model can directly interact with the execution environment.

Elaborate hand-crafted harnesses appear to yield poor returns for current MLE benchmarks. Multi-agent orchestrators and dedicated subagents add engineering and maintenance cost without consistent benchmark gains under controlled conditions.

The finding is scoped to current autonomous MLE benchmarks, equal-time comparisons, and frontier models. It does not prove harnesses are useless for longer horizons, persistent memory, safety constraints, enterprise workflows, or weaker models that need more structured support.
report.impact: The result challenges a common assumption in agent development: that more orchestration, retrieval, and multi-agent structure automatically produces better outcomes. For the AI industry, it shifts attention toward model capability, evaluation quality, and simple, robust tool interfaces rather than increasingly complex scaffolds. Developers can simplify architectures, benchmark against minimal coding-agent baselines, and avoid sunk costs in bespoke harnesses that may not generalize. Regular users may benefit from cheaper, more reliable agents with fewer brittle components, though the finding also suggests that “multi-agent” marketing may overstate real performance differences. The broader lesson is to measure harness value empirically under controlled budgets instead of assuming complexity equals capability.
report.tools: To follow up, watch MLE-bench and MLAgentBench for evaluating autonomous ML engineering, and minimal coding-agent harnesses such as OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Claude Code, and Codex CLI. Lightweight frameworks like smolagents are useful for testing simple read/write/bash tool loops. Compare any elaborate multi-agent stack against a single-session minimal baseline under the same model and time budget.
